summary: Proposes a protocol for connecting host computers to ARPA-like networks through directly connected front end processors. It offers approaches using available hardware and software and acknowledges many contributors.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 647 proposes a way to connect new kinds of computers to an ARPA-like network through a front-end processor. The front end handles the network control work, while a small host module uses a five-command protocol to exchange data and connection requests.

subtitle: A proposal for connecting new host systems to a network through a front-end processor.

tldr.problem: Organizations wanted to connect computers without existing ARPANET counterparts, but developing a full NCP and host interface for each system was a major task.
tldr.mechanism: The flexible approach places a front-end processor between the Host and IMP, where it handles the NCP and communicates with a small Host-Front End Protocol module in the Host.
tldr.outcome: The authors recommend the flexible approach over simulating a known device and describe the H-FP proposal as around 90% complete.

today: The unit records RFC 647's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The RFC describes a proposed Host-Front End Protocol and does not report whether it was adopted.

sections.title: Why Put a Front End Between Host and Network
sections.content:
The RFC addresses organizations planning to connect general-purpose computers that have no direct counterpart on the ARPANET. Their host interfaces and Network Control Programs could not simply be copied from an existing system, and the authors describe building a new NCP as a major undertaking.

A small front-end processor sits between the Host and the IMP. It handles the NCP, reducing the networking work required inside the Host. The RFC compares two ways for the front end and host to interact.
sections.plainLanguage: A new computer may not know how to handle all the network's control messages. A smaller front-end machine can take on that work and pass data to the host.

sections.title: Rigid and Flexible Approaches
sections.content:
The rigid approach makes the front end imitate a familiar device, such as a remote job-entry terminal, so the Host needs no software changes. The authors argue that this limits network data to the kinds of input and output the simulated device already supports, and can rule out uses such as graphics or process-to-process communication.

The proposed flexible approach allows minimal changes to the Host. The front end handles the NCP, while an H-FP module in the Host directs data to the appropriate parts of its operating system. The authors argue that this allows the Host to add network uses as needed, rather than being limited to a simulated device.
sections.plainLanguage: A front end that imitates a known device can restrict what the host can do with network data. The flexible design gives the host a small module for directing data and can support more uses.

sections.title: The Five H-FP Commands
sections.content:
The Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP) has five commands, and either the Host or the front end may send them. BEGIN establishes a connection, ACKNOWLEDGE reports acceptance or failure, MESSAGE carries data, INTERRUPT signals an interrupt, and END terminates a connection.

Each connection has an INDEX, with zero reserved for the global Host-front-end connection. BEGIN carries information such as Host number, socket, translation type and connection type. The front end treats certain socket values specially for TELNET, FTP, RJE and host-specific batch service.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has commands to start a connection, confirm a command, send data, interrupt a process and end a connection. An index identifies which connection each command concerns.

sections.title: Host Capabilities and Proposal Status
sections.content:
The proposal allows a Host to use the H-FP fully, use the front end to manage some TELNET or FTP details, or accept only a restricted host-specific RJE/batch connection. The front end can translate character sets and manage network sockets, while the Host remains responsible for accessing its own file system if it participates in file transfer.

The authors say the protocol is around 90% complete and acknowledge that some condition codes are not specified. They recommend evaluating the flexible alternative rather than rushing to the rigid front-end approach.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can begin with a limited set of network functions and add more later. The authors present H-FP as a proposal that still needs some details completed.
